THE BUSINESS QUESTION

Can fewer handling exceptions pay for the extra calibration time, support, and integration cost?

01 / SETUP

Manual retuning

A new package or surface condition may need a new release setting. Measure technician time per changeover before claiming a saving.

02 / QUALITY

Repeat exceptions

Overshoot or a short stop may need operator help. Count interventions per 1,000 transfers and their actual handling cost.

03 / CAPACITY

Learning takes time

An extra probe can slow the process. Compare passive learning first; require a probe to justify its added cost.

01 / SCENARIO ECONOMICS

Does the idea pay for itself?

All starting values below are illustrative assumptions. Replace them with measured pilot data.

ASSUMPTIONS, NOT RESULTS

Change the assumptions

An exception is one transfer needing operator help. Use direct, non-overlapping costs. Extra time cost includes probes and any lost capacity; it must not be counted again in exception cost.

WEEK 1

Measure the baseline

Log exception rate, cycle time, changeover work, and direct cost. Agree on definitions and a minimum worthwhile effect.

WEEK 2

Validate off the line

Measure release speed and stopping error on a guarded test fixture. Check where the simple friction model fails.

WEEKS 3-4

Run a controlled trial

Start with recommendations only. Use approved test windows and matched product groups to compare strategies.

WEEKS 5-6

Make the decision

Count exceptions and all added time. Review cost, confidence, overrides, and failure cases with Operations and Quality.

PROPOSED ACCEPTANCE GATES

Agree before collecting results.

These targets are a proposal, not industry standards or achieved results.

  • At least 20% lower intervention rate in matched product groups, with an agreed uncertainty analysis.
  • No more than 2% loss of throughput; no worsening of damage or stop events.
  • Measured costs support payback within the agreed target.
  • Every live setting change needs an approved equipment envelope, rollback, and a named owner.
PROPOSED NEXT DECISION

Approve discovery and bench testing.

Do not commit to production rollout on simulation scores or the sample ROI alone.

Prototype scope

The current world is a 1D free glide with known release speed. Belt contact, jams, vision, PLC control, and physical safety systems are outside the implemented model. No live equipment is connected.

WHAT THE DATA SAYS

Shared cases

Friction ranges from 0.10 to 0.75. Start, target, and position noise also vary. All strategies share each case and the same noise at each move index. The limit is six moves.

Counting costs

Averages include failed runs. Time is sliding time plus 0.35 s per move. Input energy is Σ½mv² for a 1 kg box. It is not motor power use.

Reading the results

Wilson intervals describe each success rate. A claim about a significant difference between strategies needs a separate paired test.

OPEN IMPLEMENTATION

See the decisions.Check the results.

A small physics model, a range of possible answers, and tests you can rerun.

Download source ↓
01 / WORLD MODEL

Keep several possible answers.

The model assigns probabilities to 81 friction values from 0.08 to 0.80. After each glide, it uses noisy start and end positions to update those probabilities.

d = v₀|v₀| / (2μg)
p(μ | D) ∝ p(D | μ) p(μ)

The error model includes two position readings, a 3 mm fixed allowance, and 2.5% of predicted distance. Each update keeps 1% of the starting belief. A large prediction error reopens the starting range. These choices do not guarantee accurate 95% intervals when the model is wrong.

02 / ACTIVE IDENTIFICATION

Choose a move that teaches.

When friction uncertainty is high, the model compares six release speeds. It weighs expected information against motion cost. It rejects a candidate if its estimated chance of crossing the boundary is above 0.1%.

score(a) = I(μ; Δx | a, D)
− 3 E[|Δx|] − 0.03 v₀²

It probes only when the best score is above 0.25. Otherwise it takes a task move. This is a practical rule, not an optimal dual-control solver. Its safety estimate depends on the model being right.

03 / REPLAN AFTER EACH MOVE

Predict, act, and plan again.

The planner compares 64 candidate speeds and predicts one full glide. After the box stops, it reads a new position and replans. It does not optimize a multi-step action sequence.

Fixed modelKeeps one friction value.

Passive adaptationPlans with the current belief and learns after each task move.

Active adaptationAdds the option to take a probe.

Robust planningPlans for the worst case across the full friction range.

04 / INDEPENDENT PHYSICS

Check with two worlds.

The browser integrates motion numerically. Python can use the same controller design with MuJoCo gravity and frictional contact.

The MuJoCo box can move along x and z, with rotation locked. Setting its initial speed represents the release. There is no robot arm or camera model.

World→ noisy position →Model + planner→ speed →World

The controller only accepts an allowlisted setup and observations. Tests check the data boundary and agreement between Python and JavaScript.

GET IT RUNNING

Run your own tests.

Python 3.10+ and Node.js 18+. MuJoCo physics runs here need no GPU or OpenGL renderer.

Setup and project guide ↗
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e '.[mujoco,test]'

python -m awm.cli demo --engine mujoco
python -m awm.cli benchmark --engine mujoco --n 100
pytest -q
npm ci
npm test

# Serve the browser demo.
python -m http.server 8080 --directory dist
